q: Which two approaches does 2.1 give for solving linear regression?
choices: Gradient descent and the normal equation
Gradient descent and the sigmoid function
The normal equation and one-vs-all
Polynomial features and regularization
why: Slide 3 sets up the lecture as gradient descent (iterative) vs the normal equation θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy (closed form).

q: With n features, the multivariable hypothesis is…
choices: h(x) = θ₀ + Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ θᵢxᵢ
h(x) = θ₀ · Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ θᵢxᵢ
h(x) = Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ θᵢ + xᵢ
h(x) = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₁x²
why: Each feature gets its own weight; n is the number of features. For the deck's 3-feature data it is θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂ + θ₃x₃. The last option is polynomial in a single x.

q: Why add a column x₀ = 1 to the data?
choices: So θ₀ becomes an ordinary weight and h(x) = Xθ works as one product
So that every feature is scaled to the same range before training
So the matrix XᵀX becomes the identity and needs no inversion
So the cost J(θ) can never become exactly zero during training
why: θ₀x₀ = θ₀ when x₀ = 1, so the intercept folds into the matrix product h(x) = Xθ.

q: A dataset has 5 examples and 3 features. After adding the x₀ column, what are the shapes of X and θ?
choices: X is 5×4, θ is 4×1
X is 5×3, θ is 3×1
X is 4×5, θ is 5×1
X is 5×4, θ is 5×1
why: One row per example and one column per feature plus the ones column gives 5×4. θ needs one entry per column (4×1), so Xθ is 5×1, one prediction per example.

q: θ = [32, 1.8, 0, 0] and one row of X is [1, 10, 12, 5]. What is the prediction h(x)?
why: 1·32 + 10·1.8 + 12·0 + 5·0 = 32 + 18 = 50, which matches y = 50 for that row. The normal-equation model predicts exactly 50 for this input.

q: θ = [1, 2, 0, 1] and x = [1, 3, 5, 2] (x₀ = 1 first). What is h(x) = xθ?
Temperature data y = [50, 59, 68, 77, 86], starting θ = 0 (so every prediction is 0). What is J(θ)?
why: The squared residuals sum to 2500 + 3481 + 4624 + 5929 + 7396 = 23930, and 23930/(2·5) = 2393. 4786 divides by m only; 340 is Σy.

q: What is the vectorised gradient-descent update for linear regression?
choices: θ := (XᵀX)⁻¹·Xᵀ·(h(x) − y)
why: Xᵀ(h − y) gives every partial sum Σ(h − y)·xⱼ in one product. You need Xᵀ, not X, for the shapes to match; the sign is minus to go downhill; and the last option mixes in the normal equation.

q: In the worked example Xᵀ(h − y) = [−340, −7250, −7635, −1845], with α = 0.001 and m = 5. What is θ₁ after one step from θ = 0?
why: θ₁ = 0 − 0.001·(1/5)·(−7250) = 1.45. 7.25 forgets the 1/m, −1.45 drops the minus sign, and 0.068 is θ₀.

q: Same step: the first entry of Xᵀ(h − y) is −340. What is θ₀ after the update, exactly?
why: 0.001·(1/5)·340 = 0.068. The slide prints 0.06 (truncated), but its next predictions such as 34.737 were computed with 0.068.

q: In the 2.1 example, what does the first entry of Xᵀ(h − y) equal?
choices: The plain sum of the residuals, because the x₀ row of Xᵀ is all ones
The sum of the squared residuals divided by twice the number of examples
The residual of the first training example multiplied by its x₁ value
The mean of the target vector y, because θ starts at zero
why: The first row of Xᵀ is [1,1,1,1,1], so that entry is Σ(h − y) = −340: the θ₀ gradient before the 1/m.

q: How did J change over the first three gradient-descent iterations in 2.1 (α = 0.001)?
why: After the first update the predictions jump from 0 to about 35–93, so J drops sharply to 62.625 and then to 61.25. It keeps falling (about 14 by iteration 900 in the code).

q: What is the normal equation?
choices: θ = (Xᵀ·X)⁻¹·(Xᵀ·y)
θ = (X·Xᵀ)⁻¹·(X·y)
θ = (Xᵀ·y)⁻¹·(Xᵀ·X)
θ = Xᵀ·(X·θ − y)
why: It solves for the optimal θ in one shot. The order matters: invert XᵀX, then multiply by Xᵀy.

q: For a design matrix X with a leading ones column and m = 5 rows, what is the top-left entry of XᵀX?
why: That entry is the dot product of the ones column with itself, Σ1 = m = 5. The slide's XᵀX starts with 5, and its next entry 100 is Σx₁.

q: In the 2.1 example, what is the first entry of Xᵀy?
choices: 340, the sum of all targets
50, the first target
68, the mean target
5, the number of examples
why: The ones row of Xᵀ times y adds up the targets: 50 + 59 + 68 + 77 + 86 = 340.

q: The normal equation returns θ = [32, 1.8, 2.8e−14, −1.7e−13]. How should you read the last two values?
choices: As floating-point noise: those features carry no information
As small but real weights that slightly improve predictions
As a sign the matrix inversion failed and θ is invalid
As the learning rate and number of iterations it used
why: Values around 10⁻¹⁴ are numerically zero. The model recovered F = 32 + 1.8·C exactly and correctly ignores x₂ and x₃.

q: Which is true of the normal equation compared with gradient descent?
choices: No learning rate and no iterations, but very slow with very many features
Needs a learning rate, but works best when there are very many features
Needs many iterations, but never has to invert any matrix at all
No learning rate, and it is fastest when there are very many features
why: Normal equation: no α, no iterations, must compute (XᵀX)⁻¹, slow when n is large. Gradient descent: choose α, many iterations, very good with many features.

q: You have a very large number of features. Which method does 2.1 recommend, and why?
choices: Gradient descent, because computing (XᵀX)⁻¹ becomes too slow
Normal equation, because it needs no learning rate to tune
Normal equation, because it finishes without any iterations
Gradient descent, because the normal equation needs a learning rate
why: No α and no iterations are real advantages of the normal equation, but inverting XᵀX gets very slow as n grows. That is where gradient descent wins.

q: In the 2.1 code, what does X_fin = np.hstack((np.ones((5,1)), X)) do?
choices: Adds the x₀ = 1 column, turning a 5×3 X into 5×4
Stacks y under X to form one 10×3 array
Normalises X so each column has mean 0
Transposes X from 5×3 into a 3×5 matrix
why: hstack places the ones column beside the 3 features, giving the (5, 4) design matrix printed on the slide.

q: In the training loop, which lines implement one gradient-descent step?
choices: delta = np.dot(X_fin.T, error); theta = theta − learning_rate*delta/m
delta = np.dot(X_fin, error); theta = theta + learning_rate*delta*m
delta = np.sum(error**2)/(2*m); theta = theta − learning_rate*delta
delta = np.linalg.inv(X_fin.T.dot(X_fin)); theta = delta.dot(error)
why: That is θ := θ − α·(1/m)·Xᵀ(h − y). The third option computes the loss, not the gradient; the fourth is the normal equation.

q: In the linear_regression notebook's normalization section, how is the test set standardised?
choices: With the training set's mean and standard deviation
With the test set's own mean and standard deviation
With the mean and std of the train and test sets combined
It isn't: only the training inputs are standardised
why: The notebook computes x_mean and x_std on x_train and reuses them for x_test ('use train mean/std for test too').

q: What is the 'core trick' of polynomial regression?
choices: Build new features x², x³, … from x, then train ordinary linear regression on them
Replace the squared-error cost with a polynomial cost of the same degree
Fit a separate straight line to each region of x and join them together
Apply the sigmoid to x before fitting so the curve can bend smoothly
why: Original feature x → extension x, x², x³ → linear model w₁x + w₂x² + w₃x³ + b. The solver is unchanged.

q: Is the model w₁x + w₂x² + w₃x³ + b linear or nonlinear?
choices: Linear in the parameters w; 'polynomial' describes only the features
Nonlinear in w, so it needs a completely different solver
Linear in x, because every power of x is added together
Nonlinear in both x and w, so the normal equation fails
why: The key point on the slide: the model is still linear with respect to w. That is why linear regression machinery, gradient descent or the normal equation, still works.

q: What does PolynomialFeatures(degree=2) map a single input x to?
choices: [x, x²]
[x², x⁴]
why: The code comment on the slide: PolynomialFeatures: x -> [1, x, x^2]. The 1 is the bias column.

q: In poly_model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree=2), LinearRegression()), what does make_pipeline do?
choices: Chains the steps into a single model you can fit and predict with
Splits the data into separate training and test pipelines
Runs both models in parallel and averages their predictions
Searches automatically for the best polynomial degree
why: It combines feature generation and regression into one model, 'convenient and error-free'. It does not choose the degree for you.

q: The slide calls degree 'the main hyperparameter — it must be chosen correctly'. What goes wrong with a degree that is far too high?
choices: The curve overfits: it follows the training points but generalises badly
The curve underfits: it stays a straight line whatever the data shows
Training cannot start because PolynomialFeatures rejects high degrees
Nothing changes, because the model stays linear in its parameters
why: Too high a degree overfits (high variance); too low underfits (high bias). 2.2's housing example shows a degree-4 curve wiggling through every point.

q: A polynomial model has w₁ = 1, w₂ = 2, w₃ = 0, b = 1. What does it predict at x = 2?
why: w₁x + w₂x² + w₃x³ + b = 2 + 2·4 + 0 + 1 = 11. 7 uses 2x instead of x², and 6 forgets b.

q: In binary classification with y ∈ {0, 1}, what does y = 0 denote in the tumour example?
choices: The negative class: a benign tumour
The positive class: a malignant tumour
An unlabelled example to be ignored
A tumour whose size is exactly zero
why: 0 is the 'negative class' (benign) and 1 is the 'positive class' (malignant). Multi-class labels look like y ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}.

q: Why does thresholding a linear regression fit at 0.5 fail for tumour classification?
choices: One far-away point tilts the line and moves the 0.5 crossing, misclassifying others
The 0.5 threshold can only be applied to models trained on images, not sizes
Linear regression cannot be fitted to labels that are only 0 or 1 at all
The fitted line is always horizontal when every label is 0 or 1
why: Adding one large malignant tumour flattens the fitted line, so the 0.5 point shifts right and earlier malignant cases are now predicted benign.

q: What output range does logistic regression guarantee that linear regression does not?
choices: h_θ(x) ≥ 0 only
why: A linear h can be above 1 or below 0, which makes no sense as a probability. The sigmoid keeps outputs between 0 and 1. It outputs a probability, not a hard 0/1.

q: What is the logistic (sigmoid) function?
why: h_θ(x) = g(Xθ) = 1/(1 + e^(−Xθ)). The third option equals 1 − g(z), which is the mirror image.

q: What is g(0) for the sigmoid?
why: g(0) = 1/(1 + e⁰) = 1/2. That is why every prediction is 0.5 when θ starts at zero. 0.693 is the resulting cost, not the output.

q: Using e^(−ln 3) = 1/3, what is g(ln 3)?
As z → +∞ and z → −∞, the sigmoid g(z) approaches…
choices: 1 and 0
0 and 1
+∞ and −∞
why: It is an S-curve squashing all reals into (0, 1): near 1 for large positive z and near 0 for large negative z, crossing 0.5 at z = 0.

q: What does h_θ(x) = 0.7 mean for a patient with x = [1, tumorSize]?
choices: An estimated 70% chance that the tumour is malignant (y = 1)
An estimated 70% chance that the tumour is benign (y = 0)
The tumour is 70% of the size threshold for malignancy
The model is wrong on 70% of the training examples
why: h_θ(x) = P(y = 1 | x; θ), the estimated probability of the positive class, which here is malignant.

q: If h_θ(x) = P(y = 1 | x; θ) = 0.7, what is P(y = 0 | x; θ)?
why: The two probabilities sum to 1, so P(y = 0) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.

q: To predict y = 1 with logistic regression, which check is enough?
choices: Xθ ≥ 0
Xθ ≥ 1
why: g(z) ≥ 0.5 exactly when z ≥ 0, so you can skip the sigmoid and check the sign of Xθ. 0.5 is the threshold on h, not on z. e^(−z) ≥ 1 means z ≤ 0, the opposite.

q: h_θ(x) = g(θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂) with θ = [−3, 1, 1]. What is the decision boundary?
choices: x₁ + x₂ = 3
x₁ + x₂ = −3
x₁ + x₂ = 0.5
x₁ = x₂
why: Set −3 + x₁ + x₂ = 0. Predict y = 1 when x₁ + x₂ ≥ 3 and y = 0 when x₁ + x₂ < 3. On the line, h_θ(x) = 0.5.

q: With θ = [−3, 1, 1], what is predicted for the point (x₁, x₂) = (1, 1)?
choices: y = 1, since 1 + 1 > 0
y = 1, since g(−1) > 0
It lies exactly on the boundary
why: z = −1 < 0, so h = g(−1) < 0.5 and the prediction is 0. The point is below the line x₁ + x₂ = 3. g(−1) is positive, but it is below 0.5.

q: With θ = [−3, 1, 1], what is h_θ(x) at the point (2, 1)?
why: z = −3 + 2 + 1 = 0 and g(0) = 0.5: the point lies exactly on the decision boundary x₁ + x₂ = 3.

q: θ = [−4, 2, 0] for h = g(θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂). Where is the decision boundary?
choices: The vertical line x₁ = 2
The horizontal line x₂ = 2
The line x₁ + x₂ = 4
The vertical line x₁ = −2
why: −4 + 2x₁ = 0 gives x₁ = 2; x₂ has weight 0 so it plays no part. Predict 1 when x₁ ≥ 2.

q: What is the logistic regression cost for a single example?
choices: −log(h_θ(x)) if y = 1;  −log(1 − h_θ(x)) if y = 0
−log(1 − h_θ(x)) if y = 1;  −log(h_θ(x)) if y = 0
½(h_θ(x) − y)² for both y = 1 and y = 0
log(h_θ(x)) if y = 1;  log(1 − h_θ(x)) if y = 0
why: This log loss is 0 when you predict the right class with certainty and grows without bound as you approach the wrong one. The last option has the sign wrong, so the cost would be negative.

q: y = 1 but the model outputs h_θ(x) close to 0. What happens to the cost?
choices: It shoots toward infinity: confident and wrong is punished hardest
It approaches 0, because log of a small number is small
It is capped at 1, as it is for any wrong prediction
It equals 0.693, as it does for any wrong prediction
why: For y = 1 the cost is −log(h), and −log(h) → ∞ as h → 0. The y = 1 curve on the slide rises steeply near h = 0.

q: Which single formula combines both cases of the logistic cost?
choices: −y·log(h_θ(x)) − (1 − y)·log(1 − h_θ(x))
−y·log(1 − h_θ(x)) − (1 − y)·log(h_θ(x))
−log(h_θ(x)) − log(1 − h_θ(x))
y·log(h_θ(x)) + (1 − y)·log(1 − h_θ(x))
why: When y = 1 the second term vanishes; when y = 0 the first vanishes. The last option is missing the minus sign.

q: Which cost function does 2.2 use for logistic regression?
choices: Log loss averaged over examples, −(1/m)Σ[y log h + (1 − y) log(1 − h)]
The squared-error cost (1/2m)Σ(h − y)², the same as linear regression
The absolute error (1/m)Σ|h − y| between prediction and label
The count of misclassified examples divided by m
why: Logistic regression replaces squared error with log loss. Only the gradient-descent update ends up looking like linear regression's.

q: One example has y = 0 and the model outputs h = 0.5. What is its cost?
why: For y = 0 the cost is −log(1 − 0.5) = −log 0.5 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693. 0.25 is the squared error, which logistic regression doesn't use.

q: y = 1 and the model outputs h_θ(x) = 1. What is the cost?
why: −log(1) = 0. A perfectly confident correct prediction costs nothing. ∞ is the y = 1, h → 0 case.

q: θ starts at all zeros for a 5-example logistic problem. What is the first value of J(θ)?
why: Every h = g(0) = 0.5 and every example costs −log 0.5 ≈ 0.693, so the average is 0.693 (= ln 2). A useful check: starting from zero weights, the first cost should be 0.693.

q: How does the logistic regression gradient-descent update compare with linear regression's?
choices: Same form, θ := θ − α(1/m)Xᵀ(h − y); only h is now the sigmoid of Xθ
Completely different: it needs second derivatives of the log loss
Same form, except the sign flips to + because of the minus in log loss
Same form, but logistic regression has no 1/m factor in the update
why: The update is identical in form; what changed is h_θ(x) = 1/(1 + e^(−Xθ)) instead of Xθ. (Slides 17 and 25 drop the 1/m in the sum form, but the boxed vectorised rule on slide 26 has it.)

q: θ = 0 and y = [1, 0, 0, 1, 1]. What is h(x) − y on the first iteration?
why: Every h is 0.5, so h − y is 0.5 − 1 = −0.5 where y = 1 and 0.5 − 0 = 0.5 where y = 0.

q: In 2.2's example Xᵀ(h − y) = [−0.5, 1.5, −3.5], with α = 0.1, m = 5 and θ = 0. What is θ after one step?
why: α/m = 0.02, so the step is 0.02·[−0.5, 1.5, −3.5] = [−0.01, 0.03, −0.07], and θ = 0 − step = [0.01, −0.03, 0.07]. The second option forgets to subtract; the third forgets the 1/m.

q: Two examples: x⁽¹⁾ = [1, 0], y⁽¹⁾ = 1 and x⁽²⁾ = [1, 2], y⁽²⁾ = 0. Starting from θ = [0, 0] with α = 0.2, what is θ₁ after one step?
why: h = 0.5 for both, so h − y = [−0.5, 0.5]. The θ₁ gradient is (1/2)(−0.5·0 + 0.5·2) = 0.5, so θ₁ = 0 − 0.2·0.5 = −0.1. (θ₀'s gradient is 0.)

q: What happened to J over the first three iterations of 2.2's worked example?
why: The cost falls each iteration, as it should. 2393 → 62.6 → 61.25 is the linear regression example from 2.1.

q: Which is one of 2.2's multi-class classification examples?
choices: Email foldering into Work, Friends, Family, Hobby
Email filtering into Spam or Not spam
Tumour detection as Benign or Malignant
Transactions flagged as Fraud or Not fraud
why: Multi-class examples: email foldering (4 classes), medical diagnosis Not ill/Cold/Flu, and weather Sunny/Cloudy/Rain/Snow. The others are binary.

q: How does one-vs-all (one-vs-rest) handle a problem with 3 classes?
choices: Train 3 binary logistic classifiers, one per class against all the others
Train 1 logistic classifier whose output is rounded to 1, 2 or 3
Train 2 classifiers and treat the leftover examples as the third class
Train 3 classifiers, one for each pair of classes, and take a vote
why: Each h⁽ⁱ⁾_θ(x) estimates P(y = i | x; θ) for its class versus the rest, so K classes need K classifiers. A pairwise vote is not the method taught.

q: Three one-vs-all classifiers output h⁽¹⁾ = 0.2, h⁽²⁾ = 0.7, h⁽³⁾ = 0.4 for a new x. Which class is predicted?
choices: Class 2
Class 1
Class 3
None, since no output is above 0.8
why: Pick the class i that maximises h⁽ⁱ⁾_θ(x): the largest output wins, with no extra threshold.

q: In the 2.2 one-vs-all code, how is the label vector prepared to train the classifier for class c?
choices: y_c = np.where(y == c, 1, 0): class c becomes 1, every other class 0
y_c = y / c, so that class c's labels become exactly 1
y_c = y[y == c], keeping only the examples that belong to class c
y_c = np.argmax(y), so each example is labelled with the top class
why: Each binary classifier sees its class as positive and the rest as negative. Prediction later uses np.argmax over the sigmoid outputs.

q: How does 2.2 define overfitting?
choices: Fitting the training set very well (J ≈ 0) but failing to generalise to new examples
Failing to fit even the training set because the model is far too simple
Training for so many iterations that the cost starts rising again
Using a learning rate so large that gradient descent diverges
why: With too many features the hypothesis can drive training cost near zero yet predict new prices badly. Too simple a model is underfitting.

q: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Underfit → high bias; overfit → high variance
Underfit → high variance; overfit → high bias
Underfit → low bias; overfit → low variance
Underfit → high bias; overfit → low variance
why: The straight line θ₀ + θ₁x underfits (high bias). The degree-4 curve through every point overfits (high variance).

q: In 2.2's housing-price example, which hypothesis is shown as the good fit?
choices: θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x²
θ₀ + θ₁x
θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x² + θ₃x³ + θ₄x⁴
θ₀ alone
why: The quadratic follows the data. The straight line underfits and the quartic wiggles through every point (overfits).

q: What are 2.2's two options for addressing overfitting?
choices: Reduce the number of features, or apply regularization
Increase the learning rate, or run more iterations
Add more polynomial features, or remove the bias term
Switch to the normal equation, or lower the threshold
why: Option 1: reduce features (manually, or with a model-selection algorithm later in the course). Option 2: regularization.

q: What does regularization do, according to 2.2?
choices: Keeps all features but shrinks the magnitude of the parameters θⱼ
Removes the least useful features before training begins
Rescales every input feature to lie between 0 and 1
Adds more training examples so the model sees more data
why: It adds a penalty term to the cost so weights stay small, which improves generalisation. It works well when many features each contribute a bit to predicting y.

q: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization penalties?
choices: L1 (Lasso) adds λΣ|θⱼ|; L2 (Ridge) adds λΣθⱼ²
L1 (Ridge) adds λΣ|θⱼ|; L2 (Lasso) adds λΣθⱼ²
L1 (Lasso) adds λΣθⱼ²; L2 (Ridge) adds λΣ|θⱼ|
L1 adds λ·m; L2 adds λ·m², with no θ involved
why: L1 = Lasso = absolute values of the weights; L2 = Ridge = squares of the weights.

q: Linear regression with L2 regularization is better known as…
choices: Ridge regression
Lasso regression
Logistic regression
Stepwise regression
why: Slide 45: Linear Regression (L2-regularization) → Ridge Regression. Lasso is the L1 version.

q: In the L2 penalty Σⱼ θⱼ², why does the sum start at j = 1?
choices: The bias θ₀ is not regularized, so it gets its own update without λ
θ₀ is always zero, so including it would change nothing
Indexing starts at 1 in the formula, but θ₀ is still penalised
θ₀ is the learning rate, so it cannot be squared
why: The penalty runs over θ₁…θₙ. That is why the gradient-descent rules write θ₀'s update separately, with no λ term.

q: θ = [θ₀, θ₁, θ₂] = [5, 1, 2] and λ = 1. What is the L2 penalty λΣⱼ₌₁ⁿ θⱼ²?
why: Skip θ₀: 1² + 2² = 5. 30 wrongly includes θ₀² = 25; 3 sums without squaring (that is the L1 penalty).

q: Which term does L2 add to the logistic regression cost?
choices: + (λ/2m)·Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ θⱼ²
+ (λ/2m)·Σⱼ₌₀ⁿ θⱼ²
− (λ/m)·Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ |θⱼ|
+ λ·Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ (h − y)²
why: The regularized logistic cost is the log loss plus (λ/2m)Σθⱼ² from j = 1, where λ is the regularization parameter. Starting at j = 0 would wrongly penalise the bias.
